Masti’s literary universe was shaped by both Indian tradition and Western literary ideals. His characters were often drawn from rural life and historical settings, reflecting his keen observation of society. Alongside fiction, he also wrote plays, essays, biographies, and poems. He edited the monthly journal

from 1944 to 1965, which became a platform for emerging writers. His biography of Muddu Krishna was particularly well-received, showcasing his skill in blending historical research with literary flair.

Masti was a strong advocate of linguistic and cultural pride. Despite being fluent in English and well-read in Western classics, he chose to write almost entirely in Kannada. He played a central role in popularizing the language as a medium of serious literature. His works encouraged generations of writers to embrace Kannada and use it to explore universal themes. He was honored with several awards including the Padma Bhushan in 1954 for his contributions to literature and education.

Beyond his literary and administrative work, Masti led a disciplined, scholarly life, deeply rooted in ethics and Gandhian simplicity. He remained active in literary circles well into his 90s.
